sections.h: What God asked Israel to build
sections.b:
Exodus 25–31 gives the plan, in seven speeches of God to Moses on the mountain, and 35–40 tells how it was built. The structure had three zones of growing holiness: a linen-walled courtyard (about 150 by 75 feet) with the bronze altar and basin; a tent with an outer room holding the table of Presence Bread, the gold lampstand and the incense altar; and an inner cube, the most holy place, holding the ark with its atonement lid and cherubim. Woven curtains, goat-hair cloth and two layers of leather covered a frame of gilded acacia wood standing on silver bases cast from the people's ransom money (30:11–16; 38:25–27). Every piece could be taken apart and carried.

The purpose is stated at the start and fulfilled at the end: "They are to make me a holy place, and I will live in their midst" (25:8); "the LORD's glory filled the tabernacle" (40:34).
sections.refs: Exodus 25:8–9; Exodus 26:1–37; Exodus 27:9–19; Exodus 30:11–16; Exodus 38:25–27; Exodus 40:34–35

sections.b: Traditional Jewish and Christian readers take the tabernacle as a real tent built at Sinai. Conservative scholars (Kitchen, Hoffmeier) compare Egyptian portable shrines and gilded frame buildings, and Michael Homan points to Ramesses II's war camp at Kadesh (about 1274 BC), whose royal tent had the same two-to-one plan, a layout an exilic writer would hardly have known. Critics reply that such tent camps lasted into the Iron Age, so the parallel does not date the text. Daniel Fleming has shown that Mari used a large tent for worship about 1800 BC, so the idea of a tent sanctuary is old. Julius Wellhausen called the tabernacle a projection of Solomon's temple into the desert by the priestly writers (P). Menahem Haran also saw the Jerusalem temple behind it, but he, Yehezkel Kaufmann, Jacob Milgrom and Israel Knohl date P before the exile, while many others date it to the exile or after. Frank Moore Cross linked it with David's tent for the ark, and Richard Friedman argued that it was set up inside Solomon's temple. The text itself presents the design as a heavenly pattern shown to Moses (25:9, 40), which is how Hebrews reads it.
sections.refs: Exodus 25:9; Exodus 25:40; Exodus 26:30; 2 Samuel 6:17; 2 Samuel 7:6; 1 Samuel 2:22; Hebrews 8:5

sections.b: Many scholars have traced links between the tabernacle story and Genesis 1–2: seven divine speeches ending with the Sabbath (25:1–31:17); a craftsman filled with the Spirit of God and with the wisdom by which God made the world (31:3); the work "finished," "seen" and "blessed" (39:32, 43); Moses "finished the work" (40:33); and the dedication on New Year's Day (40:2). On this reading the world is God's first temple, and the tabernacle is a world in small. Between the plan and the building stands the golden calf, a kind of second fall, so the building becomes a new start after sin.
sections.refs: Exodus 25:1; Exodus 31:3; Exodus 31:12–17; Exodus 39:32; Exodus 39:43; Exodus 40:2; Exodus 40:33; Genesis 1:31–2:3

sections.b: The rabbis read the building as both history and teaching. From the pairing of the building with the Sabbath (31:12–17; 35:1–3) they defined the 39 kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath. Rashi held that the tabernacle was commanded after the calf as a sign of forgiveness; Ramban held that it was God's first intention and a portable Sinai, carrying the mountain's glory with the people. After the temple fell, the synagogue and the home table came to be seen as small sanctuaries, and the weekly Torah readings Terumah, Tetzaveh, Vayaqhel and Pequdei keep the tabernacle in the yearly cycle.
sections.refs: Exodus 25:1–9; Exodus 31:12–18; Exodus 35:1–3; Exodus 40:34–38

sections.b: The New Testament takes the tabernacle as a pattern pointing to Christ. John writes that the Word "pitched his tent (eskēnōsen) among us. We gazed at his glory" (John 1:14). Hebrews argues that the tent was "an outline and a shadow" of the heavenly sanctuary (Hebrews 8:5), that its two rooms showed the way into God's presence was not yet open (9:8), and that Christ entered the true holy place with his own blood (9:11–12), opening "a fresh and living way ... through the veil, that is, his flesh" (Hebrews 10:20). Church writers from Origen to Bede read each furnishing as a picture of Christ or the church, and Revelation ends with the cry, "God's tent is with human beings" (Revelation 21:3).
sections.refs: John 1:14; Hebrews 8:1–5; Hebrews 9:1–14; Hebrews 10:19–22; Revelation 15:5; Revelation 21:3

common: The tabernacle was a large building (it was a tent about 45 by 15 feet inside, in a courtyard about 150 by 75 feet).
Anyone could go inside (only priests entered the tent, and only the high priest the inner room, once a year).
uncommon: The ark's poles were never removed, and their ends were still visible in Solomon's temple (Exodus 25:15; 1 Kings 8:8).
The bases the tabernacle stood on were cast from the census silver, the ransom paid equally by every man (Exodus 38:25–27).

claude.title: The calf as a counterfeit tabernacle
claude.body: My own reading, which overlaps with observations by Cassuto, Childs and others: the golden calf is told as a point-by-point parody of the tabernacle. Both begin with a collection of gold from the people (25:2–3; 32:2–3); both are made by a craftsman (Bezalel; Aaron with a tool, 32:4); both have an altar (27:1; 32:5); both lead to burnt offerings and peace offerings (29:28; 32:6) and a festival "for the LORD" (32:5). The difference is that one is commanded and the other invented, one hides God behind a veil and the other puts a god on display. Read this way, chapters 25–40 are a single story about two ways of having God present.

sections.b: The ark is the first item God describes (25:10–22) because it is the heart of the tabernacle: a chest of acacia wood covered with gold, about 45 by 27 by 27 inches, with rings and permanent poles for carrying. Inside lay "the testimony," the stone tablets of the covenant (25:16; 40:20). Over it sat the gold atonement lid, the kapporet, with two cherubim whose wings sheltered it. God promised to meet and speak with Moses "from between the two cherubim" (25:22). Together the lid and cherubim formed an empty throne for the invisible God, and the ark was called his footstool. Bezalel made it first among the furnishings (37:1–9), and Moses placed the tablets in it on the day the tabernacle was raised (40:20–21).
sections.refs: Exodus 25:10–22; Exodus 37:1–9; Exodus 40:20–21; 1 Samuel 4:4; 1 Chronicles 28:2

common: The ark held the manna and Aaron's staff (Hebrews 9:4 says so, but 1 Kings 8:9 says only the tablets were in it in Solomon's day).
uncommon: Ark means simply "chest"; the Hebrew word for Noah's ark and Moses' basket is a different one.

sections.h: Cherubim over the ark and on the curtains
sections.b: In Exodus two gold cherubim are hammered out of one piece with the ark's lid, facing each other with wings spread over it (25:18–20; 37:7–9). Cherubim are also woven into the inner curtains and the veil (26:1, 31), so that the priest inside was surrounded by them, as Eden's entrance was guarded by them (Genesis 3:24). Ancient Near Eastern art shows winged sphinxes beside royal thrones, which helps explain why the LORD is called the one "who sits on the cherubim as his throne" (1 Samuel 4:4). The Talmud said the cherubim faced each other when Israel did God's will (Bava Batra 99a).
sections.refs: Exodus 25:18–22; Exodus 26:1; Exodus 26:31; Exodus 37:7–9; Genesis 3:24; 1 Samuel 4:4; Psalm 80:1

common: Cherubs are chubby baby angels (that image comes from Renaissance art, not the Bible).
uncommon: The Talmud says the cherubim turned toward or away from each other depending on Israel's faithfulness (Bava Batra 99a).

sections.b: Forty days after Sinai, the people decide Moses is not coming back and demand that Aaron "make us gods that will go ahead of us" (32:1). He casts a calf from their gold earrings, builds an altar and announces "a festival for the LORD" (32:4–5). God tells Moses and threatens to destroy the people; Moses pleads and God relents (32:7–14). Moses comes down, smashes the tablets, destroys the calf and makes the people drink its dust (32:15–20). The Levites kill about three thousand (32:25–29), a plague follows (32:35), and Moses intercedes again, offering his own life (32:30–33). Through Moses' prayers in chapters 33–34 God agrees to go with the people, reveals his name and renews the covenant.
sections.refs: Exodus 32:1–35; Exodus 33:12–17; Exodus 34:6–10

sections.b: King Jeroboam set up gold calves at Bethel and Dan and said, "Here are your gods, Israel, that brought you up from the land of Egypt!" (1 Kings 12:28), nearly the same words as Exodus 32:4. Traditional readers see Jeroboam repeating Aaron's sin. Many critical scholars think the Exodus story was told or retold in Judah to condemn the northern shrines. Many also think the calves were meant as pedestals for the invisible God, like the cherubim, rather than images of another god, which would make the sin a breach of the second commandment more than the first. Hosea mocks "the calf of Samaria" (Hosea 8:5–6), and Psalm 106:20 says Israel "traded their glory for the shape of an ox that feeds on grass."
sections.refs: Exodus 32:4–5; 1 Kings 12:26–33; Hosea 8:5–6; Hosea 10:5; Psalm 106:19–23; Nehemiah 9:18

sections.b: The rabbis called the calf Israel's original sin, and said every later punishment contained a small share of it (Sanhedrin 102a). They also softened it: the mixed crowd from Egypt led it, the women refused their earrings, Aaron stalled for time after seeing Hur killed (Sanhedrin 7a). Rashi held that the tabernacle was given afterward as atonement, and Jewish tradition dates Moses' return with the second tablets to Yom Kippur. Christian writers used the story to warn against idolatry (1 Corinthians 10:7, quoting Exodus 32:6) and, in Stephen's speech, as an example of Israel's resistance to God (Acts 7:39–41), a use that later fed anti-Jewish polemic. Modern Jewish and Christian readers alike stress that the story is told by Israel against itself, as a confession.
sections.refs: Exodus 32:1–6; Exodus 32:24; Exodus 34:29; Acts 7:39–41; 1 Corinthians 10:7

common: The people abandoned the LORD for a different god (Aaron calls it "a festival for the LORD," 32:5, and many think the calf was meant to represent or carry the LORD).
uncommon: Deuteronomy says God was angry enough with Aaron to destroy him, and only Moses' prayer saved him (Deuteronomy 9:20).

claude.title: Two collections of gold
claude.body: My own observation, close to points made by Childs and others: the book puts two collections side by side. For the calf, Aaron demands gold and the people strip it off at once (32:2–3). For the tabernacle, God asks only for willing gifts and the people bring so much they must be stopped (35:21–29; 36:5–7). The generosity is the same; what changes is the object. The story seems to say that Israel's problem was never a lack of devotion, but devotion aimed at something it had made for itself.

sections.b: Exodus 32–34 is the Bible's great intercession. When God says "leave me alone" so that he can destroy the people and start again with Moses (32:10), Moses refuses the offer and argues: they are your people, whom you brought out (32:11); the Egyptians will mock (32:12); you swore to Abraham, Isaac and Israel (32:13). God relents (32:14). Moses then offers his own life ("wipe me out, please, from your book," 32:32), insists that God's own presence go with them (33:12–16), and asks to see God's glory (33:18). The result is the revelation of God's merciful name (34:6–7) and a renewed covenant. The rabbis said God's "leave me alone" was an invitation to pray (Berakhot 32a), and Psalm 106:23 says Moses "stood in the broken wall facing him."
sections.refs: Exodus 32:7–14; Exodus 32:30–34; Exodus 33:12–17; Exodus 34:8–9; Numbers 14:11–20; Psalm 106:23; Deuteronomy 9:18–20

common: Prayer cannot change anything God has said he will do (Exodus says God relented in response to Moses, 32:14, though theologians explain this differently).
uncommon: Moses turns God's own reason for staying away ("they are stiff-necked") into his reason for coming (34:9).

sections.h: Face to face, yet only his back
sections.b: Exodus 33 holds two claims side by side. The LORD spoke with Moses "face to face, as anyone talks with a close companion" (33:11), yet when Moses asks to see God's glory, God says, "You cannot see my face, for no human being can see me and stay alive" (33:20). Moses is hidden in a crack in the rock, covered by God's hand, and sees only God's "back" as he passes (33:22–23). What he receives in place of sight is God's name and character (34:5–7). The Talmud said Moses saw the knot of God's tefillin; Maimonides said he saw God's effects, not his essence; Gregory of Nyssa said to see God's back is to follow him; Luther spoke of God known from behind, in suffering and the cross. John 1:18 answers from the Christian side: "Nobody has ever seen God. It is the only one, God, the one in the Father's embrace, who has made him known."
sections.refs: Exodus 24:10–11; Exodus 33:11; Exodus 33:18–23; Exodus 34:5–7; Numbers 12:8; John 1:14–18

common: Moses saw God's face (Exodus says he spoke with God "face to face" but was not allowed to see his face, 33:11, 20).
uncommon: The prophet Elijah later stood at the mouth of "the cave" on the same mountain as God passed by, and the rabbis identified it with Moses' cleft (1 Kings 19:9–13).

claude.title: A God seen from behind is a God who leads
claude.body: My own suggestion: in 33:14 God promises "My face will go," and in 33:23 Moses sees only God's back. A guide who goes in front is always seen from behind. The vision on the rock may act out the promise just made: God will be with them not as an object to look at but as a leader to follow, the cloud going ahead of the camp (40:36–38). This is close to Gregory of Nyssa's reading, though he applied it to the soul's endless pursuit of God.

sections.b: In Exodus the glory (kavod) is God's visible presence: fire and cloud on Sinai (24:16–17), the goal of Moses' request "Please let me see your glory" (33:18), and the cloud that fills the finished tabernacle so completely that Moses cannot enter (40:34–35). The verb used there, shakhan, "settle," is the verb of God's first promise, "I will live in their midst" (25:8), and gives the rabbinic word Shekhinah. Moses' own face reflects the glory after he speaks with God (34:29–35), which Paul contrasts with "the knowledge of God's glory, seen in the face of Christ" (2 Corinthians 3:7–4:6). The book ends with the glory traveling with Israel by cloud and fire (40:36–38).
sections.refs: Exodus 24:16–17; Exodus 29:43; Exodus 33:18–23; Exodus 34:29–35; Exodus 40:34–38; 1 Kings 8:10–11; John 1:14; 2 Corinthians 3:7–18

common: "Shekhinah" is a Bible word (it is a later rabbinic word, built on the verb shakhan used in Exodus 25:8 and 40:35).
uncommon: Paul's verb in 2 Corinthians 3:13, often translated "fading," more likely means "being set aside"; Exodus never says Moses' glory faded.

sections.b: Exodus 28–29 creates Israel's priesthood. Aaron and his four sons are chosen (28:1), dressed in holy clothes "for glory and for beauty" (28:2), and ordained in a seven-day rite of washing, dressing, anointing and sacrifice, with blood on the right ear, thumb and toe (29:1–37). The high priest's clothes carry the people with him: their names on his shoulders and over his heart (28:12, 29), the Urim and Thummim for God's decisions (28:30), and a gold plate reading "Holy to the LORD" so that their gifts are accepted (28:36–38). The Levites are set apart in a different way, by rallying to Moses after the calf (32:26–29). The priesthood is promised "for all time" (40:15), which Jewish tradition sees as still in force and Hebrews as fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 7:11–28).
sections.refs: Exodus 28:1–43; Exodus 29:1–46; Exodus 32:26–29; Exodus 40:12–15; Leviticus 8:1–36; Hebrews 7:11–28

common: The rope tied to the high priest's ankle (a late legend, not in the Bible or Talmud).
uncommon: The Talmud says each of the high priest's eight garments atoned for a particular sin (Zevachim 88b).

sections.h: High priest and maker of the calf
sections.b: In Exodus 25–40 Aaron has two faces. He is chosen and ordained as the first high priest, dressed in the most splendid clothes in the Bible, and given the charge of carrying Israel's names before God (28–29). He is also the one who makes the golden calf, builds its altar, proclaims its feast, and then blames the people and the fire ("out came this calf!" 32:24). The narrator twice says plainly that Aaron made it (32:4, 35). Deuteronomy adds that Moses' prayer saved him from God's anger (Deuteronomy 9:20). The rabbis defended him as a man trying to stall a mob that had already killed Hur (Sanhedrin 7a); critical scholars often see in the story a polemic against priests who claimed descent from Aaron at Bethel.
sections.refs: Exodus 28:1–4; Exodus 29:4–9; Exodus 32:1–6; Exodus 32:21–25; Exodus 32:35; Deuteronomy 9:20

common: Aaron was punished for the calf (Exodus records no punishment for him, though Deuteronomy 9:20 says only Moses' prayer saved him).
uncommon: The Samaritan Pentateuch and a Qumran scroll add Deuteronomy 9:20 into Exodus 32:10.

sections.b: Exodus mentions the Urim and Thummim once, without explaining them: they are to be put "into the breastpiece for decisions" so that Aaron carries "the decisions for the Israelites" over his heart (28:30). The building account never says they were made, a gap the Samaritan Pentateuch fills (39:21). Most scholars think they were two lots giving yes-or-no answers, as the longer Greek of 1 Samuel 14:41 suggests. Josephus said the stones shone with God's answer until about 200 years before his day; the Talmud said the letters on the breastpiece lit up (Yoma 73b). The Greek called them "the revealing and the truth," and Yale University still carries the Hebrew words on its seal.
sections.refs: Exodus 28:15; Exodus 28:30; Exodus 39:21; Leviticus 8:8; Numbers 27:21; 1 Samuel 14:41; Ezra 2:63

common: The Urim and Thummim were the twelve stones of the breastpiece (Exodus distinguishes them: the stones are set on it, the Urim and Thummim are put into it).
uncommon: The two words begin with the first and last letters of the Hebrew alphabet.

sections.h: The golden altar and the holy recipe
sections.b: A small gold-covered altar stood in front of the veil, and Aaron burned incense on it every morning and evening when he tended the lamps (30:1–8). Once a year its horns were cleansed with blood (30:10). The incense was made from four ingredients in equal parts (stacte, onycha, galbanum and frankincense), salted, pure and holy, and anyone who copied it for private use was "cut off" (30:34–38). Its odd placement, after the priests rather than with the other furniture, has led critics to see it as a later addition, and two ancient texts move it to 26:35. Archaeologists have found incense altars at Arad with frankincense residue. Psalm 141:2 and Revelation 5:8 and 8:3–4 link incense with prayer.
sections.refs: Exodus 26:35; Exodus 30:1–10; Exodus 30:34–38; Exodus 37:25–29; Exodus 40:26–27; Psalm 141:2; Revelation 8:3–4

common: The incense altar stood in the most holy place (Exodus puts it outside the veil; Hebrews 9:4 is debated).
uncommon: The Talmud lists eleven incense spices and says the foul-smelling galbanum teaches that sinners belong in the community's prayer (Keritot 6b).

sections.b: Exodus prepares for the Day of Atonement without describing it. The ark's gold lid is named kapporet, "atonement lid" (25:17), where blood will be sprinkled (Leviticus 16:14–15); the incense altar's horns are cleansed "once a year" (30:10); and the census silver is "atonement money" (30:16). Jewish tradition also roots the day in the golden calf: by the rabbis' count Moses came down with the second tablets and God's forgiveness on the tenth of the seventh month, which became Yom Kippur (Seder Olam; Rashi on 33:11). The Thirteen Attributes of 34:6–7 are recited again and again in its prayers. Hebrews 9 reads the yearly entry of the high priest as a shadow of Christ's once-for-all entry into the true sanctuary.
sections.refs: Exodus 25:17–22; Exodus 30:10; Exodus 30:16; Exodus 34:6–7; Exodus 34:29; Leviticus 16:1–34; Hebrews 9:7–12

common: "Mercy seat" is a translation of the Hebrew (it was coined by Tyndale; the Hebrew kapporet means something like "atonement lid").
uncommon: Jewish tradition dates the first Yom Kippur to Moses' return with the second tablets after the golden calf.

sections.b: The tabernacle is a map of holiness. The courtyard is open to Israelites, the holy place only to priests, and the most holy place (a perfect cube) only to the high priest once a year (26:33–34). Materials grow costlier as one moves in: bronze, silver, gold. Priests are "made holy" by washing, clothing, blood and oil (29:1–37), and "anything that touches the altar will become holy" (29:37). The anointing oil and incense are holy and must not be copied (30:32–38). Aaron wears "Holy to the LORD" on his forehead (28:36). Time is holy too: the Sabbath is "holy to the LORD," a sign that "I, the LORD, set you apart as holy" (31:13–15). Holiness here means belonging to God, and it is both a gift and a danger.
sections.refs: Exodus 26:33–34; Exodus 28:36–38; Exodus 29:37; Exodus 30:29–33; Exodus 31:13–15; Leviticus 19:2; Haggai 2:11–13

common: Holy simply means morally good (in the Bible it means first of all set apart for God).
uncommon: Hebrew says "most holy" by repeating the word: "holy of holies" (26:33).

sections.b: The gold lampstand (menorah) was hammered from a single talent of gold, about 75 pounds, into a stylized almond tree with a central shaft, six branches, and cups shaped like almond blossoms (25:31–40; 37:17–24). Its seven lamps, fed with pure pressed olive oil brought by the people, burned from evening to morning (27:20–21; 30:7–8). Many scholars, following Carol Meyers, see it as a sacred tree, perhaps the tree of life. The almond (shaqed) suggests the God who keeps watch (shoqed, Jeremiah 1:11–12). Josephus and Philo said its seven lamps stood for the seven planets. Rashi records the midrash that Moses could not picture it, so God made it come out of the fire by itself.
sections.refs: Exodus 25:31–40; Exodus 27:20–21; Exodus 37:17–24; Exodus 40:24–25; Leviticus 24:1–4; Jeremiah 1:11–12; Zechariah 4:2–14

common: The menorah of the tabernacle had nine branches (that is the Hanukkah lamp; the tabernacle's had seven lamps).
uncommon: The Arch of Titus in Rome shows the temple menorah being carried off in AD 70, and it became the emblem of the State of Israel.

sections.h: The stones of the high priest's breastpiece
sections.b: Twelve stones, each engraved with the name of one tribe, were set in four rows on the high priest's breastpiece (28:17–21; 39:10–14), and two onyx stones with six names each sat on his shoulders (28:9–12). The Hebrew names are hard to identify: ancient names often went by color, the Greek translators and Josephus already disagreed, and some traditional renderings (diamond, sapphire) name stones that could not have been engraved or were unknown in Israel. Revelation's twelve foundation stones of the new Jerusalem (21:19–20) draw on this list, so that the names of Israel's tribes worn by the high priest become the foundations of God's city.
sections.refs: Exodus 28:9–21; Exodus 39:6–14; Ezekiel 28:13; Revelation 21:19–20

sections.h: The Sabbath sign and the tabernacle
sections.b: The tabernacle instructions end with the Sabbath (31:12–17), and the building begins with it (35:1–3). The Sabbath is "a sign between me and you" and "a covenant for all time," grounded in creation: "in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, and on the seventh day he stopped and caught his breath" (31:17). Rashi drew from the opening "above all" that even building the sanctuary must stop on the Sabbath, and the rabbis defined the 39 kinds of forbidden work from the crafts used to build the tabernacle (Shabbat 49b). The ban on lighting a fire (35:3) divided Karaites, who sat in darkness, from Rabbanites, who lit candles before sunset. Verses 31:16–17, Veshamru, are sung every Sabbath.
sections.refs: Exodus 31:12–17; Exodus 35:1–3; Exodus 34:21; Ezekiel 20:12; Mark 2:27; Colossians 2:16–17

uncommon: Exodus says God "caught his breath" on the seventh day (31:17), and the Talmud built on this the idea of an "extra soul" given on the Sabbath (Beitzah 16a).

sections.b: Exodus 31–34 tells how the Sinai covenant nearly ended. God gives Moses "the tablets of the testimony" written by his own finger (31:18). Moses smashes them when he sees the calf (32:19), an act that, in ancient legal language, cancels the agreement. After Moses' intercession God has him cut new tablets (34:1), reveals his merciful name (34:6–7), and says, "Here I am, making a covenant" (34:10), restating key terms (34:11–26) and writing "the Ten Words" again (34:28). The tablets are then laid in the ark under the atonement lid (40:20). Jeremiah's later promise of a new covenant "It will not be like the covenant I cut with their ancestors... They broke that covenant of mine" (Jeremiah 31:32) looks back on this pattern of breaking and renewal.
sections.refs: Exodus 31:18; Exodus 32:15–19; Exodus 34:1; Exodus 34:10–28; Exodus 40:20; Deuteronomy 10:1–5; Jeremiah 31:31–34

uncommon: Goethe argued in 1773 that the "Ten Words" of the second tablets were the ritual laws of Exodus 34:14–26, not the Ten Commandments of chapter 20.

sections.b: After the golden calf God passes before Moses and proclaims: "The LORD, the LORD, a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love and faithfulness, keeping loyal love to thousands, forgiving guilt, rebellion and sin" (34:6–7). This is the Hebrew Bible's most-quoted description of God (Numbers 14:18; Nehemiah 9:17; Psalm 86:15; 103:8; 145:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2). Jewish tradition counts thirteen attributes of mercy in it and recites them in every prayer for forgiveness, ending the quotation at "and clears" so that it closes with pardon (Rosh Hashanah 17b; Yoma 86a). The words rachum, from "womb," and channun, "freely kind," are used almost only of God.
sections.refs: Exodus 33:19; Exodus 34:6–7; Numbers 14:18; Psalm 103:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2

common: The Old Testament God is a God of wrath and the New Testament God a God of love (God's self-description in Exodus 34:6 begins with compassion and grace).

sections.b: In God's self-revelation chesed appears twice: God is "great in loyal love and faithfulness" and "keeping loyal love to thousands" (34:6–7). The pair chesed ve'emet, "loyal love and faithfulness," is the same one used by Abraham's servant (Genesis 24:27), and many scholars hear it behind John's description of the Word "full of grace and truth" (John 1:14, 17). The contrast between love kept "to thousands" and punishment reaching "the third and fourth generation" shows which side of God's character outweighs the other (compare Deuteronomy 7:9).
sections.refs: Exodus 34:6–7; Exodus 20:6; Genesis 24:27; Deuteronomy 7:9; John 1:14–17

sections.b: In Exodus 25–40 Moses receives the tabernacle plan in a vision (25:40), smashes the tablets and destroys the calf (32:19–20), pleads for the people three times (32:11–13, 31–32; 33:12–16), meets God in the tent outside the camp "face to face, as anyone talks with a close companion" (33:11), sees God's back from a cleft in the rock (33:22–23), fasts forty days twice (34:28; Deuteronomy 9:9, 18), and comes down with a shining face that he must veil (34:29–35). He then oversees the building, inspects and blesses the work (39:43), sets up the tabernacle himself, and "finished the work" (40:33), but cannot enter when the glory fills it (40:35). Jerome's Latin rendered his shining face as "horned," which explains Michelangelo's horned Moses.
sections.refs: Exodus 25:40; Exodus 32:11–32; Exodus 33:7–23; Exodus 34:28–35; Exodus 39:43; Exodus 40:16–35; 2 Corinthians 3:7–18

common: Moses had horns (a misunderstanding of the Hebrew qaran, "shone," through the Latin Vulgate).

sections.h: The tabernacle as a new creation
sections.b: The priestly account of the tabernacle seems to have been shaped to echo Genesis 1–2. The instructions come in seven speeches, the seventh about the Sabbath (25:1; 30:11, 17, 22, 34; 31:1, 12). Bezalel is filled with the Spirit of God and with wisdom, understanding and knowledge, the gifts by which God made the world (31:3; Proverbs 3:19–20). The ending echoes the seventh day: the work "was finished" (39:32; Genesis 2:1), Moses "saw" it and "blessed" (39:43; Genesis 1:31; 2:3), and "Moses finished the work" (40:33; Genesis 2:2). Scholars such as Kearney, Blenkinsopp, Weinfeld and Levenson argue that the sanctuary is pictured as a small world, and the world as God's temple.
sections.refs: Exodus 25:1; Exodus 31:1–17; Exodus 39:32; Exodus 39:43; Exodus 40:33; Genesis 1:31–2:3

sections.b: Source critics assign chapters 25–31 and 35–40 to the Priestly source (P), with its interest in measurements, priests, holiness and the Sabbath, and chapters 32–34 mostly to older, non-priestly material (often called J and E) with later editing. They point to the different tents (the tabernacle in the center of the camp, the tent of meeting outside it in 33:7–11), the two names Horeb and Sinai, the two accounts of the punishment for the calf (32:20, 28, 35), and the "ritual decalogue" of 34:14–26. Many now see P as a late (exilic or after) layer that framed the older story. Traditional scholars answer that one author can use different styles for law, plans and narrative, and that the structure of command, sin and rebuilding is a single design.

sections.h: The tabernacle chapters in the Greek
sections.b: Exodus 35–40 is one of the places where the Septuagint differs most from the Hebrew. The Greek tells the building in another order (the priests' clothes first), is shorter, and omits the making of the incense altar and the goat-hair tent, frames and crossbars. D. W. Gooding argued for a later Greek reworking; Anneli Aejmelaeus and others for a different Hebrew original, perhaps an earlier edition. Hebrew witnesses also vary: the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Qumran scroll 4QpaleoExod-m move the incense altar passage to 26:35 and add harmonizing material, such as Deuteronomy 9:20 at 32:10. These cases show that the text of Exodus was still being shaped and copied in more than one form before the time of Jesus.
sections.refs: Exodus 26:35; Exodus 30:1–10; Exodus 32:10; Exodus 36:8–38; Exodus 37:25–28

sections.h: The tabernacle and its furnishings as types
sections.b: Christian typology found rich material in Exodus 25–40. Hebrews reads the tent as "an outline and a shadow" of the heavenly sanctuary (Hebrews 8:5) and the veil as Christ's flesh (10:20). Paul calls Christ the hilastērion, the Greek name for the atonement lid (Romans 3:25). Origen's homilies and Bede's On the Tabernacle read every board, color and ring as a picture of Christ, the church or the virtues: gold for divinity, acacia wood for incorruptible humanity, blue for heaven. Modern interpreters usually keep the New Testament's own links and treat the more detailed allegories as devotional reading rather than the meaning of the text.
sections.refs: Exodus 25:17–22; Exodus 25:40; Exodus 26:31–33; Hebrews 8:5; Hebrews 9:1–12; Hebrews 10:19–20; Romans 3:25

sections.b: In 33:19 God promises to "call out the name of the LORD" before Moses, and in 34:5–7 he does: "The LORD, the LORD, a God compassionate and gracious..." The name YHWH, first explained in 3:14–15, is now filled with content: it means mercy, grace, patience, loyal love, faithfulness, forgiveness and justice. In the same chapter God gives himself another name: "the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God" (34:14), the jealousy of a husband who will not share his bride. The words "I will show grace to whoever I show grace" (33:19) echo the pattern of "I will be who I will be" (3:14).
sections.refs: Exodus 3:14–15; Exodus 33:19; Exodus 34:5–7; Exodus 34:14

sections.h: Sacrifices in the ordination and the daily offering
sections.b: Exodus 29 introduces several kinds of offering that Leviticus explains: the chatat (sin or purification offering) that cleanses the altar and the priests, the olah (burnt offering) burned whole "as a soothing smell," the ram of ordination, and the shelamim (peace offerings) shared between God, priests and worshipers. The chapter ends with the tamid, two lambs offered every morning and evening, the rhythm on which Jewish prayer times were later based. The altar itself must be purified with blood and "atoned for" (29:36–37), showing that atonement in these texts means cleansing God's house as well as forgiving people.
sections.refs: Exodus 29:10–28; Exodus 29:36–42; Leviticus 1–7; Numbers 28:3–8; Hebrews 10:11–14

sections.b: The tabernacle is the forerunner of Solomon's temple, and the two are described in parallel: a heavenly or divine pattern (Exodus 25:9, 40; 1 Chronicles 28:11–19), Spirit-filled or skilled craftsmen from Judah and Dan or Naphtali (Exodus 31:2–6; 1 Kings 7:13–14; 2 Chronicles 2:13–14), a dedication when the cloud and glory fill the house so that no one can enter (Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:10–11), and the same furnishings on a larger scale. Critical scholars think the influence ran the other way, with the priestly picture of the tabernacle modeled on the temple. Either way, the Bible presents one line of sanctuaries from Sinai to Zion, which the New Testament extends to Christ and the church.
sections.refs: Exodus 25:8–9; Exodus 31:2–6; Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 6:1–38; 1 Kings 8:1–11; 1 Chronicles 28:11–19; John 2:19–21

sections.b: The first person the Bible describes as "filled with the Spirit of God" is not a prophet or king but an artist, Bezalel, given "skill, with understanding, with know-how, and with every kind of craft" to design and build the tabernacle (31:3; 35:31). The skilled weavers are likewise filled with "a spirit of wisdom" (28:3), and Bezalel and Oholiab are given the gift of teaching (35:34). The words echo the Spirit of God over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2) and the wisdom by which God made the world (Proverbs 3:19–20).
sections.refs: Exodus 28:3; Exodus 31:1–6; Exodus 35:30–35; Genesis 1:2; Proverbs 3:19–20

sections.b: The first mention of God's book comes in Moses' intercession after the golden calf: "But if not, wipe me out, please, from your book that you have written" (32:32). God answers, "The one who has sinned against me is the one I will wipe out of my book" (32:33). The image is of a register of the living, like a city's list of citizens. Paul's wish to be cut off for his people (Romans 9:3) echoes Moses' offer. Jewish tradition developed the picture of books opened on Rosh Hashanah and sealed on Yom Kippur (Rosh Hashanah 16b).
sections.refs: Exodus 32:32–33; Psalm 69:28; Daniel 12:1; Romans 9:3; Philippians 4:3; Revelation 3:5
